title: $10,000 Invested Equally in Alphabet and Nvidia Could Be Worth This Much by 2030
detail:
$10,000 Invested Equally in Alphabet and Nvidia Could Be Worth This Much by 2030
Micah Zimmerman, The Motley Fool
Mon, October 12, 2026 at 2:50 PM PDT 5 min read
NVDA
GOOG
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Pick almost any frontier of anything from modern tech, search, or advertising, cloud computing, self-driving cars, or quantum physics, and odds are Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOGL) (NASDAQ: GOOG) or Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) is already standing in it. Split $10,000 between the two today, and you aren't just buying a search engine and a chipmaker. You are betting that the next five years of computing will be built largely on top of what these two companies are shipping right now.

Image source: Getty Images.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Nvidia

Nvidia's second-quarter data center revenue hit $89 billion, up 117% from a year earlier. Data center revenue is simply the money Nvidia makes selling chips to the massive server farms that power AI, the physical buildings packed with computers that run everything from ChatGPT to online search and AI features. That growth came largely from Blackwell Ultra, Nvidia's current flagship chip family, ramping into the build-outs of nearly every major cloud provider on earth, meaning companies like Amazon, Microsoft, and Alphabet are all buying Nvidia hardware to stock the data centers they rent out to businesses and AI developers.

Nvidia has already moved past Blackwell in conversation, too. Its newer chip platform, called Vera Rubin, is now in full production and promises up to 10 times lower cost per AI token than Blackwell delivered. In short, a token is roughly a chunk of text an AI model processes, so a lower cost per token means it gets meaningfully cheaper to run AI software at scale, which matters enormously for whether AI companies can eventually turn a profit. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has laid out a path to $1 trillion in cumulative sales from Blackwell and Rubin combined between 2025 and 2027 alone, according to The Information. That figure would have sounded like science fiction five years ago.

Then there's another bet: quantum computing. Nvidia doesn't build quantum processors itself, but its NVQLink technology now connects quantum hardware directly to Nvidia's GPU supercomputers, and nearly every serious quantum player, from IonQ to national research labs, has started building on top of it.

Alphabet

Alphabet's core advertising and search business remains the cash engine funding everything else, but "everything else" has gotten remarkably interesting. According to Tech Crunch, Waymo, Alphabet's self-driving unit, now completes 500,000 paid robotaxi rides every week across 10 U.S. cities, up tenfold in under two years, and it's targeting 1 million weekly rides across 20 cities by the end of 2026, including its first international markets. Waymo just upsized its first-ever debt offering to $5 billion specifically to fund that global expansion, a sign Alphabet is treating this less like a moonshot experiment and more like a business it intends to scale aggressively.

Picture a $500,000 retirement position in the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (NYSEARCA:VOO). As of August 31, 2026, NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA) made up 8.08% of the fund. That puts $40,400 of your money in one semiconductor company. Would you have written a check that size to NVIDIA on purpose? For many VOO owners, the index simply made that call.

IM Imagery / Shutterstock.com
Your $500,000 Is More Lopsided Than It Looks

The concentration grows across the top ten. According to the Vanguard website, VOO's ten largest holdings carried a combined 37.78% weight, as of August 31, 2026. On a $500,000 position, that is $188,900 sitting in ten lines. Every other company in the index shares the remaining $311,100. Vanguard's prospectus counts 503 components in the target index as of December 31, 2025.

The top ten holdings belong to NVIDIA, Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL), Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT), Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN), Alphabet, Broadcom, Meta Platforms, Micron Technology, and Tesla. Alphabet takes up two separate lines because it has two share classes.

These weights are several weeks old. They shift every trading day with share prices, so the exact holdings today will show different figures.

title: Cathie Wood Calls SpaceX a "Deep-Value Opportunity" at Its IPO Price. Here's the Math She's Using.
detail:
Cathie Wood Calls SpaceX a "Deep-Value Opportunity" at Its IPO Price. Here's the Math She's Using.
Lyle Daly, The Motley Fool
Mon, October 12, 2026 at 3:20 PM PDT 4 min read
SPCX
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

When Space Exploration Technologies (NASDAQ: SPCX) went public in June, it was at a market cap of $1.75 trillion, immediately making it one of the 10 largest public companies in the world. The common read was that it was overvalued, with Morningstar valuing it at $780 billion.

Ark Invest CEO Cathie Wood disagreed. She has invested heavily in SpaceX, and in a Sept. 16 post on X, she argued that the space company could be a deep-value opportunity at its IPO price.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: The Motley Fool.
The math behind Cathie Wood's valuation

Wood and Ark analyst Sam Korus have provided calculations showing why SpaceX is a deep value, based on Starlink's revenue potential. As of 2025, Starlink generated about $19 million in annual revenue per terabit per second (Tbps) of network capacity. Each Starship carrying 60 Starlink V3 satellites adds about 61 Tbps of capacity, meaning each launch could theoretically generate $1 billion in recurring annual revenue.

SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has set a goal of 10,000 Starship launches per year by 2030. In her post on X, Wood explained that at $1 billion per launch, 10,000 flights would be $10 trillion in annual revenue.

Musk had a short reply: "It's not impossible." While that's true, Musk is known for setting extremely ambitious goals, and this one is worth a reality check.

Flaws in the argument

There are several issues with this $10 trillion revenue projection for SpaceX. The biggest: The space company is nowhere close to 10,000 Starship launches per year. The first Starship launch was in 2023, and to date, there have been 14 total, including nine successes and five failures. Even across SpaceX's fleetwide flights, the total is 165 launches in 2025 and 116 so far this year (as of Oct. 8).

SpaceX's launch cadence is impressive, as it accounts for about 80% of all U.S. orbital launches, according to recent research by The Motley Fool. But going from less than 10 Starship launches per year to 10,000 by 2030 doesn't seem realistic.

Wood's calculations also assume that every flight carries Starlink satellites and revenue per terabit holds, neither of which is likely. The 10,000-flight goal could include passenger transport, in which case it wouldn't be exclusively satellite payloads. Revenue per terabit is already declining, from $23 million in 2024 to $19 million in 2025.
